title: Amata furens. Allecto Ardeae
titleEn: Amata's Frenzy and the Fury at Ardea — Aeneid VII.373–474
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Amata's pleading has failed: Latinus stands firm, and the serpent's poison has spread through her whole body. Now the madness breaks out, and the queen rages through the city like a top that boys whip round and round an empty courtyard. She goes further. Pretending to be possessed by Bacchus, she runs out into the woods and hides her daughter Lavinia in the mountains, to keep her from the Trojans, crying that the girl belongs to the god alone. Word spreads, and the Latin mothers, caught by the same frenzy, leave their homes to follow her, hair loose to the wind, dressed in fawnskins and shrieking, while Amata holds up a blazing pine-torch and sings a wedding hymn for her daughter and Turnus, and calls on them to loose their hair and join her rites. Allecto, satisfied with this first work, flies on her dark wings to Ardea, the city Danae once founded, where Turnus lies asleep. Disguised as Calybe, an old priestess of Juno, she taunts him: will he let the Trojans have his bride and his kingdom after all his wars for Latinus? Juno herself sent her: let him arm his men and burn the Trojan ships, and let Latinus learn what Turnus is in war. Turnus laughs at her. He knows about the fleet; Juno has not forgotten him; old age is making her see phantoms, and war is men's business. Then the Fury shows herself, snakes hissing, eyes ablaze, throws his own words back at him, and hurls a burning torch into his breast. He wakes drenched in sweat, shouting for his armour; his rage boils over like a cauldron on a roaring fire. He orders his young men to march on Latinus and drive the invaders out, and the Rutulians, stirred by his youth, his beauty, his royal blood and his deeds, rush eagerly to arms.
part: Amata's Frenzy and the Fury at Ardea (VII.373–474)

sentences.t:
His ubi nequiquam dictis experta Latinum
contra stare videt penitusque in viscera lapsum
serpentis furiale malum totamque pererrat,
tum vero infelix, ingentibus excita monstris,
immensam sine more furit lymphata per urbem.
sentences.l:
When, having tried him with these words in vain, Latinus
she sees standing against her, and deep into her vitals slipped
the serpent's maddening evil, and the whole of her it roams through,
then truly the unhappy one, roused by huge monstrous sights,
through the boundless city without restraint raves, frenzied.
sentences.i: When she sees that her words have been wasted on Latinus, that he stands firm against her, while the serpent's maddening poison has slipped deep into her vitals and roams through her whole being, then indeed the unhappy queen, roused by monstrous visions, runs raving without restraint from end to end of the vast city, like one possessed.
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. 'His… dictis experta', 'having tried (him) with these words'; 'experta' is the participle of the deponent 'experior', and 'Latinum' is both its object and the subject of 'stare'. 'Ubi… videt' governs two accusative-and-infinitive clauses, 'Latinum contra stare', 'that Latinus stands against her', and 'malum… lapsum (esse)', 'that the evil has slipped'; the second then runs on into a plain indicative, 'totamque pererrat', 'and roams through all of her', a loose change of construction. 'Furiale malum', 'the Fury's evil', the snake's venom. 'Monstris', 'portents', the horrors the poison sets before her. 'Sine more', 'beyond all measure'. 'Lymphata', 'frenzied', literally 'water-maddened': the nymphs ('lymphae') were thought to strike mortals mad. 'Tum vero' marks the moment the madness, held back while she pleaded, breaks out.

sentences.i: As sometimes a top spins along beneath the twisted whip, when boys, intent on their game, drive it round and round the empty halls in a wide ring;
sentences.n: A simile, and a surprising one: a child's whipping-top. 'Ceu', 'as', is a poetic word for 'velut'. 'Quondam' here is 'at times', not 'once'. 'Turbo', 'top', anything that whirls (the same word is 'whirlwind'). 'Torto… sub verbere', 'under the twisted lash', the plaited cord of the whip. 'Vacua atria circum' puts the preposition after its noun (anastrophe): 'round the empty halls', the courts of a great house, cleared for play. 'Exercent', 'keep busy', 'keep it going'. Homer has the top in a single line (Iliad 14.413), where Ajax's stone sends Hector spinning 'like a top'; Virgil makes the image a whole scene. Amata is driven about like the top, by a force she cannot see.

sentences.t:
ille actus habena
curvatis fertur spatiis;
sentences.l:
it, driven by the thong,
is carried along in curving courses;
sentences.i: driven on by the thong, it sweeps round in curving circuits;
sentences.n: 'Ille', 'it', the top. 'Habena', usually 'rein', here the lash of the whip. 'Curvatis… spatiis', 'in curved courses': 'spatia' are the laps of a racecourse, so the language borrows from the chariot race. 'Fertur', 'is carried', passive: the top does not move of itself.

sentences.t:
stupet inscia supra
inpubesque manus, mirata volubile buxum;
sentences.l:
stands dazed, not understanding, above it
the beardless band, marvelling at the whirling boxwood;
sentences.i: the band of boys stands over it in wonder, not knowing what makes it move, marvelling at the spinning boxwood;
sentences.n: 'Stupet… manus', 'the band is dazed', a collective singular; 'inscia', 'not knowing' (what drives it). 'Supra' is an adverb, 'above', as they stand over it watching. 'Inpubes', 'not yet grown', 'beardless', is Greenough's spelling, with 'in-' left unassimilated before p (the familiar form is 'impubes'); 'inmemor' at 439 is the same. 'Mirata' (mī-rā-ta, from 'mīror') is deponent, a perfect participle with present sense, 'marvelling'. 'Volubile buxum' (vŏ-lū-), 'the spinning boxwood': tops were turned from box, a hard wood, the material naming the thing (metonymy).

sentences.t: dant animos plagae:
sentences.l: give it spirit the blows:
sentences.i: the blows put life into it:
sentences.n: 'Dant animos', 'give spirit', as if the top were a horse urged on by the whip; the plural 'animi' is usual for courage and energy. The short clause, verb first, comes like the crack of the lash, and the colon turns to the comparison's point.

sentences.t:
non cursu segnior illo
per medias urbes agitur populosque feroces.
sentences.l:
not in a course slower than that
through the midst of cities is she driven, and of fierce peoples.
sentences.i: no slower than that top is she driven through the heart of the towns and among their fierce peoples.
sentences.n: The simile is applied. 'Non… segnior', 'no slower', litotes: she goes as fast as the top. 'Illo' is ablative of comparison, 'than that (top)', with 'cursu', 'in course', ablative of respect. 'Agitur', 'is driven', passive again: the force is outside her, as with the top. 'Per medias urbes', 'through the midst of cities', a poetic plural for her own city, or the towns of the Latins as her madness spreads beyond it. 'Populos… feroces', 'fierce peoples', the warlike Latins.

sentences.t:
Quin etiam in silvas, simulato numine Bacchi,
maius adorta nefas maioremque orsa furorem
evolat et natam frondosis montibus abdit,
quo thalamum eripiat Teucris taedasque moretur,
sentences.l:
Nay more, into the woods, the godhead of Bacchus feigned,
a greater outrage having attempted and a greater frenzy begun,
she flies out, and her daughter in the leafy mountains hides,
so that she may snatch the marriage from the Teucrians and delay the torches,
sentences.i: More than that, pretending that the power of Bacchus is upon her, she ventures on a greater outrage and launches a wilder madness: she rushes out into the forest and hides her daughter in the leafy mountains, to rob the Trojans of the marriage and hold back the wedding torches,
sentences.n: 'Quin etiam', 'nay more', raises the stakes. 'Simulato numine Bacchi' is an ablative absolute, 'the godhead of Bacchus having been feigned': she pretends to be possessed by the god, and so becomes a Bacchant, whose rites took women out of the city to the mountains. 'Adorta' (from 'adorior') and 'orsa' (from 'ordior') are deponent participles, 'having undertaken', 'having begun'; 'maius… maioremque' repeats the comparative. 'Quo' with the subjunctive ('eripiat', 'moretur') is purpose, 'in order to'; prose keeps 'quo' for clauses with a comparative, verse is freer. 'Thalamum', 'bridal chamber', so 'marriage'; 'Teucris' (two syllables: eu is a diphthong) is dative of separation with 'eripiat'. 'Taedas', the pine torches of a Roman wedding procession. Euripides' Bacchae stands behind the scene: there the women of Thebes, led by royal women, rave on the mountain.

sentences.t:
Euhoe Bacche, fremens, solum te virgine dignum
vociferans, etenim mollis tibi sumere thyrsos,
te lustrare choro, sacrum tibi pascere crinem.
sentences.l:
Euhoe Bacchus, roaring, that you alone are worthy of the maiden
crying aloud, since for you she takes up the pliant thyrsi,
you she circles with the dance, the sacred hair for you she grows.
sentences.i: With a roar of Euhoe to Bacchus she shrieks that he alone is worthy of the maiden, since it is for him that the girl takes up the supple thyrsus, for him she circles in the dance, for him she lets her sacred hair grow long.
sentences.n: 'Euhoe' is the Bacchants' ritual cry (Greek 'euhoi'), 'Bacche' the vocative; Greenough prints it without speech marks, the cry being reported inside the sentence. What Amata cries is given in accusative and infinitive after 'vociferans', though she addresses the god as 'you': 'te solum… dignum (esse)', 'that you alone are worthy', with 'virgine' ablative after 'dignus', and '(eam) sumere… lustrare… pascere', 'that she (the maiden) takes up… circles… grows'. 'Mollis… thyrsos' ('-is' accusative plural), 'pliant thyrsi', the fennel wands wreathed in ivy and vine leaves. 'Te lustrare choro', 'to circle you with the dance', to honour the god with ring-dances. 'Pascere crinem', 'to let the hair grow', literally 'to feed' it: hair vowed to a god and left uncut. 'Tibi… te… tibi' is the anaphora of a hymn.

sentences.t:
Fama volat, furiisque accensas pectore matres
idem omnis simul ardor agit nova quaerere tecta:
sentences.l:
Rumour flies, and, kindled by frenzies in the breast, the mothers
the same ardour, all of them, at once drives new dwellings to seek:
sentences.i: Rumour flies, and the mothers, their hearts set ablaze with madness, are all driven at once by the same passion to go and look for new dwellings:
sentences.n: 'Fama volat', 'rumour flies': Rumour was a monstrous goddess in Book IV (4.173–197); here she is hardly more than a phrase. 'Furiis… accensas pectore', 'kindled in heart by frenzies'; 'furiis' is 'madness', with a glance at the Fury who caused it, and 'pectore' is ablative of place. 'Matres', the married women of the Latins. 'Omnis' is accusative plural ('-is' = '-es') with 'matres', 'all of them'. 'Agit… quaerere', 'drives (them) to seek', an infinitive after a verb of urging, a poetic construction. 'Nova… tecta', 'new dwellings': the woods are to be their homes.

sentences.i: they have left their homes and give their bare necks and loosened hair to the winds, while others fill the sky with trembling shrieks and, clad in fawnskins, carry spears wreathed in vine leaves;
sentences.n: 'Deseruere' is '-ere' for '-erunt', and the perfect is instantaneous: in a moment they are gone. 'Ventis dant colla comasque', 'give necks and hair to the winds': bare-necked and with hair unbound, as Bacchants were pictured. 'Ast' is an old form of 'at', 'but', kept by Virgil for weight. 'Ululatibus', 'ululations', the high wailing cry of the rites; 'aethera' is a Greek accusative. 'Incinctae pellibus', 'girt with skins', the Maenads' fawnskins, the passive participle with a middle sense, 'having girded themselves'. 'Pampineas… hastas', 'vine-leafed spears', the thyrsus seen as a weapon, which it becomes in Euripides' Bacchae; adjective and noun frame the line.

sentences.t:
ipsa inter medias flagrantem fervida pinum
sustinet ac natae Turnique canit hymenaeos,
sanguineam torquens aciem, torvumque repente
clamat:
sentences.l:
she herself, in their midst, a blazing, she burning, pine
holds up, and of her daughter and Turnus sings the wedding songs,
her bloodshot rolling gaze, and grimly, suddenly,
cries out:
sentences.i: The queen herself, on fire with passion, holds up a flaming pine-torch in their midst and sings the marriage hymn of her daughter and Turnus, rolling her bloodshot eyes; and suddenly she cries out fiercely:
sentences.n: 'Ipsa', 'she herself', the queen, at the centre of the band ('inter medias', supply 'matres'). 'Flagrantem fervida pinum', 'the blazing pine, (she) burning', two words of heat side by side, one for the torch and one for the woman. 'Pinum', 'pine', is the torch made of it: a Bacchic torch, and also the torch carried before a bride, so that her rite becomes a mock wedding. 'Hymenaeos', 'wedding songs', a Greek word, from the cry to Hymen; before it the last syllable of 'canit' is lengthened at the beat (so 'profugus hymenaeos', 10.720). 'Sanguineam torquens aciem', 'rolling her bloodshot eye'; 'acies' is the eye's keen look. 'Torvum' is a neuter adjective used as an adverb (an internal accusative), 'grimly', 'fiercely', a Greek turn Virgil likes.

sentences.t: “Io matres, audite, ubi quaeque, Latinae:
sentences.l: “Ho, mothers, hear, wherever each one is, Latin mothers:
sentences.i: “Ho, mothers of the Latins, hear me, every one of you, wherever you may be:
sentences.n: Amata's speech (400–403). 'Io' (two syllables, ĭ-ō) is a ritual shout, of joy or of summons, Greek in origin. 'Matres… Latinae', 'Latin mothers', has the vocative split by 'audite' and 'ubi quaeque', 'wherever each (of you is)', with the verb left out, so that the call goes out to every corner. The colon introduces what she wants of them.

sentences.t:
Siqua piis animis manet infelicis Amatae
gratia, si iuris materni cura remordet,
solvite crinalis vittas, capite orgia mecum.”
sentences.l:
If any for unhappy Amata in loyal hearts remains
goodwill, if for a mother's right care gnaws you,
loosen the ribbons of your hair, take up the rites with me.”
sentences.i: if any kindness for unhappy Amata still lives in your loyal hearts, if concern for a mother's rights pricks at you, loose the ribbons from your hair and join with me in the holy rites.”
sentences.n: 'Siqua' is Greenough's single word for 'si qua', 'if any' (the Latin Library divides it); 'qua' is the indefinite 'aliqua' after 'si', agreeing with 'gratia'. The capital after the colon is Greenough's way where a colon opens what is said (so 2.150, 5.28), not a misprint; the English runs on. 'Piis animis', 'in loyal hearts', ablative of place; 'pius' covers duty to kin. 'Infelicis Amatae' is an objective genitive with 'gratia', 'goodwill toward Amata': she names herself in the third person, like a figure of tragedy. 'Iuris materni cura', 'concern for a mother's right', her claim to dispose of her daughter's hand. 'Remordet', 'gnaws again', 'troubles'. 'Crinalis vittas', 'hair ribbons', the fillets of a respectable matron: to loose them is to become a Bacchant. 'Orgia', a Greek neuter plural, 'secret rites'. Amata's speech ends.

sentences.t:
Talem inter silvas, inter deserta ferarum,
reginam Allecto stimulis agit undique Bacchi.
sentences.l:
Such, among the woods, among the wilds of the beasts,
the queen Allecto with goads drives on every side, of Bacchus.
sentences.i: So, through the forests and the lonely haunts of wild beasts, Allecto drives the queen on every side with the goads of Bacchus.
sentences.n: 'Talem… reginam', 'the queen, such as she was', the adjective held a line apart from its noun, each word leading its line. 'Inter… inter', anaphora. 'Deserta ferarum', 'the wild places of the beasts', a neuter plural adjective used as a noun with a genitive. 'Stimulis… Bacchi', 'with the goads of Bacchus': the frenzy she feigned (385) is now real, and it is Allecto, not the god, who drives it. 'Agit' takes up 'agitur' (384): the queen is still the whipped top.

sentences.t:
Postquam visa satis primos acuisse furores
consiliumque omnemque domum vertisse Latini,
sentences.l:
After she seemed enough the first frenzies to have sharpened
and the plans and the whole house to have overturned of Latinus,
sentences.i: When she judged that she had whetted these first frenzies enough and turned upside down the plans and the whole household of Latinus,
sentences.n: Allecto turns from the palace to Turnus. 'Visa (est)', 'she seemed (to herself)', with the subject of the infinitives understood: 'that she had sharpened… had overturned'. 'Acuisse', 'to have whetted', as a blade. 'Primos… furores', 'the first frenzies', those begun in Amata; a further task awaits her after Turnus. 'Consiliumque omnemque domum', 'both the counsel and the whole house', with the double '-que… -que'; 'Latini', at the line's end, governs both. 'Vertisse', 'to have overturned'.

sentences.t:
protinus hinc fuscis tristis dea tollitur alis
audacis Rutuli ad muros, quam dicitur urbem
Acrisioneis Danae fundasse colonis,
praecipiti delata noto.
sentences.l:
at once from here on dusky the grim goddess rises wings
to the bold Rutulian's walls, which city it is said
with Acrisian settlers Danae founded,
on the headlong south wind carried down.
sentences.i: at once the grim goddess rises from there on her dusky wings and, swept down on a headlong southern wind, makes for the walls of the bold Rutulian, the city which Danae is said to have founded with settlers of Acrisius's people.
sentences.n: 'Tollitur', 'lifts herself', the passive with a middle sense. 'Fuscis… alis', 'on dusky wings', goes round 'tristis dea tollitur'. 'Audacis Rutuli', 'of the bold Rutulian', Turnus, named by his people; 'audax' is his standing epithet, 'daring', not always to his credit. 'Quam… urbem' sets the antecedent inside the relative clause: 'the city which'. 'Fundasse' is contracted from 'fundavisse'. Danae, daughter of Acrisius of Argos, was set adrift in a chest with her infant son Perseus; Italian legend brought her to Latium, where she founded Ardea with Argive settlers ('Acrisioneis', an adjective from Acrisius; 'Danae' is three syllables, Dă-nă-ē). This is the descent Amata claimed for Turnus (372). 'Praecipiti… noto', 'on the headlong south wind'; 'notus' (short o), the south wind, is printed lowercase as a common noun.

sentences.i: Our forefathers once called the place Ardea, and Ardea is still a great name, but its fortune is a thing of the past;
sentences.n: 'Avis' is the dative of 'avi', 'grandfathers', 'forefathers', as agent with the passive participle: 'called by our forefathers', not 'by birds'. 'Ardea' means 'heron'; Ovid, at the end of his Aeneas story (Metamorphoses 14), tells how a heron flew up from the ashes of the burned town, but Virgil leaves the tale untold. 'Et nunc manet', 'even now remains'; 'magnum… nomen' is in apposition with 'Ardea'. 'Fortuna fuit', 'its fortune has been', that is, is over: the perfect 'fuit', 'has been (and is no more)', is the idiom of 'fuimus Troes' (2.325). Ardea in Virgil's day was a decayed little town.

sentences.t:
tectis hic Turnus in altis
iam mediam nigra carpebat nocte quietem.
sentences.l:
here in the lofty house Turnus
already the middle of his rest in the black night was taking.
sentences.i: here Turnus, in his lofty palace, was already deep in sleep in the black of night.
sentences.n: 'Tectis… in altis', 'in the high house', a plural for singular, framing 'hic Turnus'. 'Carpebat… quietem', 'was taking his rest', literally 'plucking', 'enjoying': 'carpere' is the usual verb for taking sleep, or a journey, bit by bit. 'Mediam… quietem', 'the middle of his sleep': he was sound asleep. 'Nigra… nocte' is ablative of time. The imperfect sets the scene the Fury breaks into.

sentences.t:
Allecto torvam faciem et furialia membra
exuit, in vultus sese transformat anilis;
sentences.l:
Allecto her grim face and Fury's limbs
puts off, into the features she transforms herself of an old woman;
sentences.i: Allecto sheds her fierce face and the limbs of a Fury and changes herself into the features of an old woman;
sentences.n: 'Exuit', 'puts off', the verb for taking off clothes: the Fury's form is shed like a garment. 'Furialia membra', 'Fury's limbs'. 'Anilis', 'of an old woman', an adjective from 'anus', agreeing with 'vultus' ('-is' accusative plural). The Homeric model is the deceiving Dream that stood at Agamemnon's head in the likeness of Nestor (Iliad 2.20–21); in the Aeneid, Iris took the shape of old Beroe to set the Trojan women burning the ships (5.618–620).

sentences.t:
et frontem obscenam rugis arat, induit albos
cum vitta crinis, tum ramum innectit olivae;
sentences.l:
and her foul brow with wrinkles she ploughs, puts on white
hair with a ribbon, then a branch she twines in of olive;
sentences.i: she furrows her hideous brow with wrinkles, puts on white hair bound with a ribbon, and twines a sprig of olive in it;
sentences.n: 'Obscenam', 'ill-omened', 'foul': the Fury's face is still there under the disguise. 'Rugis arat', 'ploughs with wrinkles', a bold metaphor. 'Induit albos… crinis', 'puts on white hair', as if it were a wig; 'crinis' is '-is' accusative plural. 'Cum… tum', 'both… and also', the second the weightier. The ribbon ('vitta') and the olive sprig are a priestess's marks, and the olive is also the sign of peace, worn by the bringer of war. 'Innectit', 'twines in', with 'olivae' a genitive, 'a branch of olive'.

sentences.t:
fit Calybe Iunonis anus templique sacerdos
et iuveni ante oculos his se cum vocibus offert:
sentences.l:
she becomes Calybe, Juno's old woman and the temple's priestess,
and to the youth before his eyes with these words presents herself:
sentences.i: she becomes Calybe, aged priestess of Juno's temple, and presents herself before the young man's eyes with these words:
sentences.n: 'Fit Calybe', 'she becomes Calybe' (Că-lў-bē), the name of a priestess otherwise unknown, of Juno's temple at Ardea presumably. 'Iunonis anus', 'Juno's old woman', her aged servant, explained by 'templique sacerdos'. Juno fits: she is the goddess behind Allecto, and Calybe will claim to speak for her (428). 'Iuveni ante oculos', 'before the youth's eyes', 'iuveni' a dative of reference where English uses a possessive. 'His… cum vocibus', 'with these words', with 'cum' set between adjective and noun, as often in verse.

sentences.t:
“Turne, tot incassum fusos patiere labores
et tua Dardaniis transcribi sceptra colonis?
sentences.l:
“Turnus, so many labours, poured out in vain, will you endure,
and your sceptre to Dardanian settlers to be made over?
sentences.i: “Turnus, will you stand by and see so many labours poured out for nothing, and your sceptre signed over to Dardanian settlers?
sentences.n: The Fury's speech in Calybe's voice (421–434). 'Patiere' = 'patieris', 'will you endure', the future of the deponent 'patior' with the short second-person ending '-re'; it takes accusative and infinitive, '(tot labores) fusos (esse)', 'that so many labours have been spent', and 'sceptra transcribi', 'that your sceptre is transferred'. 'Incassum', 'in vain', 'for nothing'. 'Transcribi', 'to be made over', a legal word for transferring property by deed; 'colonis', 'settlers', dative, sharpens the insult: newcomers are being handed a king's title. 'Sceptra', plural for singular. Turnus's 'labours' are presumably wars fought on Latinus's side.

sentences.t:
Rex tibi coniugium et quaesitas sanguine dotes
abnegat, externusque in regnum quaeritur heres.
sentences.l:
The king to you the marriage and the dowry won with blood
refuses, and a foreign heir for the kingdom is sought.
sentences.i: The king denies you the marriage and the dowry you won with your blood, and an heir from abroad is being sought for the throne.
sentences.n: 'Tibi' is dative with 'abnegat', 'refuses (to) you'. 'Coniugium', 'marriage', with Lavinia; the princess is not named. 'Quaesitas sanguine dotes', 'a dowry sought with blood', presumably earned in battles for Latinus; 'dotes' is plural for one dowry, here the kingdom that comes with the bride. 'In regnum', 'for the kingdom'. 'Externus… heres', 'a foreign heir', twists Faunus's oracle of 'sons-in-law from abroad' (7.98): what was foretold as fate is told to Turnus as a slight. 'Quaesitas… quaeritur', the same verb twice: what he sought with blood is now sought elsewhere.

sentences.t: I nunc, ingratis offer te, inrise, periclis;
sentences.l: Go now, to thankless offer yourself, mocked one, dangers;
sentences.i: Go on, then, you dupe, and throw yourself into dangers that earn no thanks;
sentences.n: 'I nunc', 'go now', a sarcastic imperative, 'go on, then', as Dido flung at Aeneas, 'i, sequere Italiam' (4.381). 'Inrise' is the vocative of the participle 'inrisus', 'mocked', 'made a fool of', in Greenough's unassimilated spelling (familiar 'irrise'). 'Ingratis… periclis', 'to thankless dangers', goes round 'offer te, inrise'; 'periclis' is the shortened form of 'periculis', common in verse. 'Offer te', 'offer yourself', with the dative.

sentences.t: Tyrrhenas, i, sterne acies; tege pace Latinos.
sentences.l: The Tyrrhenian, go, lay low, battle lines; shelter with peace the Latins.
sentences.i: Go, cut down the Etruscan armies; keep the Latins safe in peace.
sentences.n: 'I' again, thrust inside the phrase 'Tyrrhenas… acies', 'the Etruscan battle lines': the repeated command mocks. 'Tyrrhenas', 'Tyrrhenian', Etruscan: Turnus, it is implied, has fought the Etruscans for Latinus. 'Sterne', 'strew', 'lay low'. 'Tege pace Latinos', 'shelter the Latins with peace', bitterly: he wins by his wars a peace that others will enjoy. The sting comes after the semicolon.

sentences.t:
Haec adeo tibi me, placida cum nocte iaceres,
ipsa palam fari omnipotens Saturnia iussit.
sentences.l:
These very things to you me, while in the quiet night you lay,
herself openly to speak all-powerful Saturnia ordered.
sentences.i: These are the very words that Saturn's all-powerful daughter herself bade me speak to you plainly as you lay in the quiet night.
sentences.n: 'Adeo' after 'haec' stresses it: 'these very things'. 'Me… fari… iussit', 'ordered me to speak', 'iubeo' with accusative and infinitive. 'Cum… iaceres', 'while you lay', a 'cum' clause of circumstance with the imperfect subjunctive. 'Palam', 'openly', in plain words, not riddles. 'Saturnia', 'daughter of Saturn', Juno's regular title; 'omnipotens' Virgil gives to Juno as well as to Jupiter. 'Ipsa', 'herself': this is no old woman's notion. The claim, for once in a disguise, is true.

sentences.t:
Quare age et armari pubem portisque moveri
laetus in arma para, et Phrygios qui flumine pulchro
consedere duces pictasque exure carinas.
sentences.l:
Therefore come, and the youth to be armed and from the gates to be moved
gladly to arms prepare, and the Phrygian, who by the lovely river
have settled, chieftains and their painted keels burn up.
sentences.i: So come, make ready with a glad heart to arm your young men and march them out of the gates to war, and burn up the Phrygian chieftains who have settled by the lovely river, and their painted ships.
sentences.n: 'Quare age', 'so come', 'age' an interjection of urging. 'Para' takes the passive infinitives 'armari… moveri', 'prepare the youth to be armed and moved out of the gates', a poetic construction; 'portis' is ablative of separation. 'Laetus', 'glad', an adjective doing an adverb's work. 'In arma', 'to arms', is Greenough's reading; the Latin Library prints 'in arva', 'into the fields', the open country beyond the gates, which gives the march somewhere to go and avoids 'armari… arma'; both make sense. 'Phrygios… duces', 'the Phrygian chieftains', frames the relative clause 'qui flumine pulchro consedere', 'who have settled by the lovely river', the Tiber; 'consedere' is '-ere' for '-erunt'. 'Exure', 'burn up', has two objects, men and ships, a harsh yoking (zeugma). 'Pictas… carinas', 'painted keels', ships.

sentences.t: Caelestum vis magna iubet.
sentences.l: Of the heavenly ones the great power commands.
sentences.i: The mighty will of heaven commands it.
sentences.n: 'Caelestum' is the shortened genitive plural, 'of the heavenly ones' (= 'caelestium'), a poetic form. The short sentence closes the argument with the gods' authority.

sentences.t:
Rex ipse Latinus,
ni dare coniugium et dicto parere fatetur,
sentiat et tandem Turnum experiatur in armis.”
sentences.l:
The king himself, Latinus,
unless to give the marriage and to obey his word he agrees,
let him feel it, and at last let him try Turnus in arms.”
sentences.i: As for King Latinus himself, unless he consents to grant the marriage and keep his word, let him feel the cost, and learn at last what Turnus is in arms.”
sentences.n: 'Ni', an old form of 'nisi', 'unless'. 'Fatetur', 'acknowledges', 'agrees' to 'give the marriage and obey his word', his promise to Turnus. The present indicative in the 'if' clause with a command in the main clause makes a lively mixed condition. 'Sentiat… experiatur' are jussive subjunctives, 'let him feel… let him try'. 'Turnum experiatur in armis', 'let him make trial of Turnus in arms', learn what Turnus is as an enemy: the threat is against the king himself. The speech ends.

sentences.t:
Hic iuvenis vatem inridens sic orsa vicissim
ore refert:
sentences.l:
Here the youth, mocking the prophetess, thus words in turn
from his mouth returns:
sentences.i: At this the young man, laughing at the prophetess, gave her answer in his turn:
sentences.n: 'Hic', 'at this', 'hereupon'. 'Vatem', 'the seer', 'prophetess': Calybe has spoken as one inspired. 'Inridens', 'laughing at', in Greenough's unassimilated spelling (familiar 'irridens'). 'Orsa', 'things begun', the perfect participle of 'ordior' used as a noun, 'words'; 'sic orsa… ore refert', 'thus he returns words with his mouth', a formal epic introduction. 'Vicissim', 'in turn'. His mockery, 'inridens', answers her 'inrise' (425), and will be paid back.

sentences.t:
“Classis invectas Thybridis undam
non, ut rere, meas effugit nuntius auris.
sentences.l:
“That fleets have sailed into the Tiber's water,
not, as you think, has the news escaped my ears.
sentences.i: “The news that ships have sailed into the waters of the Tiber has not, as you suppose, escaped my ears.
sentences.n: Turnus's speech (436–444). 'Classis invectas (esse)', 'that fleets have been carried into', accusative plural ('-is' = '-es') and infinitive depending on 'nuntius', 'the news', which carries the sense of a verb of saying; 'Thybridis undam', 'the Tiber's water', is the accusative of goal with 'invectas'. 'Thybris' is the Greek-style name of the Tiber. 'Rere' = 'reris', 'you think', from 'reor', with the short second-person ending. 'Meas… auris' ('-is' accusative plural) is the object of 'effugit'. Turnus is calm and dismissive: he knows the facts and does not fear them.

sentences.t: Ne tantos mihi finge metus;
sentences.l: Do not such great fears for me invent;
sentences.i: Do not dream up such terrors for me;
sentences.n: 'Ne… finge', 'do not fashion', a prohibition with 'ne' and the imperative, poetic and old-fashioned (prose has 'noli' with the infinitive, or 'ne' with the perfect subjunctive). 'Mihi', 'for me', a dative of reference. 'Fingere', 'to shape', 'to invent': he thinks the old woman is making things up.

sentences.t:
nec regia Iuno
inmemor est nostri.
sentences.l:
nor is royal Juno
unmindful of us.
sentences.i: Queen Juno has not forgotten us.
sentences.n: 'Regia Iuno', 'royal Juno', queen of the gods. 'Inmemor… nostri', 'unmindful of us', with an objective genitive; 'inmemor' is Greenough's unassimilated spelling (familiar 'immemor'), and 'nostri' is plural for singular. Line 439 is one of Virgil's unfinished half-lines (two feet and a syllable), left incomplete when he died with the Aeneid unrevised. The irony is heavy: Juno has indeed not forgotten him, and that is his ruin.

sentences.t:
Sed te victa situ verique effeta senectus,
o mater, curis nequiquam exercet et arma
regum inter falsa vatem formidine ludit.
sentences.l:
But you, overcome by mould and of truth worn out, old age,
O mother, with cares in vain keeps busy, and amid the arms
of kings with false dread you, a prophetess, mocks.
sentences.i: But it is old age, mother, gone to rust and too worn out to bear the truth, that troubles you with idle worries and fools you, the would-be prophetess, with false terrors amid the wars of kings.
sentences.n: 'Victa situ', 'overcome by mould', 'by rust': 'situs' is the decay of things left unused, here of an old mind. 'Veri effeta', 'exhausted of truth', barren of it, a genitive with an adjective of want; 'effetus' is used of a woman past childbearing. 'O mater', 'mother', a polite address to an old woman. 'Exercet', 'busies', 'harasses' (the word of the boys and their top, 380). 'Arma regum inter', 'among the arms of kings', the preposition after its noun. 'Vatem… ludit', 'mocks (you, a) prophetess', 'vatem' in apposition to 'te': he tells her she is fooled in the very role she plays. 'Falsa… formidine', 'with false dread', ablative of means. The Fury will throw this back at him word for word (452–453).

sentences.t: Cura tibi divom effigies et templa tueri:
sentences.l: Your care is the gods' images and temples to guard:
sentences.i: Your business is to look after the images of the gods and their temples:
sentences.n: 'Cura tibi (est)' (short final a in 'cura', so 'tibi' takes a long final i), 'it is a care to you', 'it is your task', a dative of possession with the verb left out; the infinitive 'tueri', 'to guard', is the subject. 'Divom' is the old genitive plural (= 'divorum'), familiar by now. 'Effigies', accusative plural, 'images', the cult statues. Turnus is sending the priestess back to her temple.

sentences.t: bella viri pacemque gerent, quis bella gerenda.”
sentences.l: wars men and peace will carry on, by whom wars are to be waged.”
sentences.i: war and peace will be the concern of men, whose task it is to wage war.”
sentences.n: 'Bella… pacemque gerent', 'will carry on war and peace': 'gerere' serves for both. 'Quis' = 'quibus', the old dative-ablative plural of the relative, 'by whom wars must be waged', with the gerundive 'gerenda (sunt)' and a dative of agent. 'Bella… bella' rings the line. The model is Hector sending Andromache back to her loom with the words that war will be the business of men (Iliad 6.490–493); Turnus says it to a priestess, and she is a Fury. The speech ends.

sentences.t:
Talibus Allecto dictis exarsit in iras,
at iuveni oranti subitus tremor occupat artus,
deriguere oculi:
sentences.l:
At such words Allecto blazed up into wrath,
but the youth, as he spoke, a sudden trembling seizes in the limbs,
stiffened his eyes:
sentences.i: At words like these Allecto flared into fury; and while the young man was still speaking, a sudden trembling seized his limbs and his eyes stared rigid:
sentences.n: 'Talibus… dictis', ablative of cause, 'at such words'. 'Exarsit in iras', 'blazed out into anger', the plural 'iras' for fits of rage. 'Iuveni oranti', 'the youth as he spoke', a dative with 'occupat artus' where English says 'his limbs'; 'orare' here has its old sense, simply 'to speak'. 'Deriguere' is '-ere' for '-erunt', 'grew stiff', an instantaneous perfect after the present 'occupat': the change of tense gives the jolt of shock.

sentences.t:
tot Erinys sibilat hydris
tantaque se facies aperit;
sentences.l:
with so many the Erinys hisses snakes,
and so great her face shows itself;
sentences.i: so many were the snakes the Fury hissed with, so huge the face she now revealed;
sentences.n: 'Tot… hydris', 'with so many water-snakes', ablative of means; 'hydra' is a Greek word, used of serpents in general. 'Erinys' is the Greek name for a Fury. 'Tot… tantaque' gives the reason he froze: so many snakes, so vast a face. 'Se… aperit', 'reveals itself', the disguise gone.

sentences.t:
tum flammea torquens
lumina cunctantem et quaerentem dicere plura
reppulit et geminos erexit crinibus anguis
verberaque insonuit rabidoque haec addidit ore:
sentences.l:
then, flaming, rolling
her eyes, him faltering and trying to say more
she thrust back, and twin she reared from her hair snakes,
and her lashes cracked, and with raving mouth these words added:
sentences.i: then, rolling her fiery eyes, she drove him back as he faltered and tried to say more, reared up two snakes from her hair, cracked her whip, and from her raving mouth added these words:
sentences.n: 'Flammea… lumina', 'flaming eyes', 'lumina' being the usual poetic word for eyes. 'Cunctantem et quaerentem', '(him) hesitating and trying', with 'eum' left out; 'quaerere' with an infinitive, 'to seek to', is poetic. 'Reppulit', 'drove back', the perfect of 'repello', with doubled p. 'Geminos… anguis' ('-is' accusative plural), 'twin snakes'; 'crinibus' is ablative of separation, 'from her hair', which is serpents. 'Verbera… insonuit', 'made her lashes resound', an intransitive verb with an internal accusative: the whip is the Fury's emblem, as the lash was the top's (378). 'Rabido… ore', 'with raving mouth'.

sentences.t:
“En ego victa situ, quam veri effeta senectus
arma inter regum falsa formidine ludit.
sentences.l:
“Look, I am she, overcome by mould, whom, of truth worn out, old age
amid the arms of kings with false dread mocks.
sentences.i: “See, here I am, the one gone to rust, whom old age, too worn out to know the truth, fools with false terrors amid the wars of kings.
sentences.n: Allecto's speech (452–455). 'En', 'look!', 'behold'. She throws his words (440–442) back at him almost verbatim, 'victa situ… veri effeta senectus… arma inter regum… falsa formidine ludit', with 'ego (sum)' and 'quam' recasting them: his scorn returns as menace. The verb 'sum' is left out. 'Arma inter', the preposition after its noun, just as he had it.

sentences.t: Respice ad haec:
sentences.l: Look back at these:
sentences.i: Look at these:
sentences.n: 'Respice ad haec', 'look at these', at her snakes and her torch. 'Respicere' is properly 'to look back' or 'to turn and look at': what he waved aside he must now face.

sentences.t:
adsum dirarum ab sede sororum,
bella manu letumque gero.”
sentences.l:
I am here from the seat of the dread Sisters,
wars in my hand and death I carry.”
sentences.i: I come from the dwelling of the dread Sisters, and in my hand I carry war and death.”
sentences.n: 'Adsum', 'I am here', 'I have come'. 'Dirarum… sororum', 'of the dread Sisters', the three Furies, Allecto, Tisiphone and Megaera, also called the 'Dirae'; 'ab sede', 'from the seat', the underworld. 'Bella manu letumque gero', 'I carry wars and death in my hand', the torch she is about to throw; 'gero' answers his 'bella… gerent, quis bella gerenda' (444): it is she who carries war. Line 455 is another of Virgil's unfinished half-lines (compare 439), three and a half feet. The speech ends.

sentences.t:
Sic effata facem iuveni coniecit et atro
lumine fumantis fixit sub pectore taedas.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, a torch at the youth she hurled, and with black
light smoking she fixed beneath his breast the brands.
sentences.i: With these words she flung a torch at the young man and drove it deep into his breast, a brand smoking with murky light.
sentences.n: 'Effata', 'having spoken', from the deponent 'effor'. 'Facem… coniecit' ('coniecit' is three syllables, con-iē-cit), 'hurled a torch', 'iuveni' a dative, 'at the youth'. 'Atro lumine fumantis… taedas', 'brands smoking with black light', an oxymoron: the light of the Fury's torch is darkness. 'Taedas' is plural for singular, the same torch as 'facem'; 'fumantis' is '-is' accusative plural. 'Fixit sub pectore', 'planted it deep in his breast': the torch is the madness she plants, as the snake was in Amata. Juno had promised funeral 'taedae' for the new Troy (321–322); here is the first.

sentences.t:
Olli somnum ingens rumpit pavor, ossaque et artus
perfundit toto proruptus corpore sudor;
sentences.l:
For him sleep a huge breaks, terror, and his bones and limbs
drenches, over his whole body bursting forth, sweat;
sentences.i: An overwhelming terror breaks his sleep, and sweat bursting out over his whole body drenches him to the bone;
sentences.n: 'Olli' is the archaic form of 'illi', 'for him', a dative of reference; Virgil keeps it, after Ennius, for solemn moments. 'Ingens… pavor', 'huge dread', frames 'rumpit'. 'Proruptus… sudor', 'sweat burst forth', the participle with middle sense. 'Toto… corpore', ablative of place. Turnus wakes: the Fury came to him in sleep, as Homer's dreams come.

sentences.t: arma amens fremit, arma toro tectisque requirit;
sentences.l: Arms, out of his mind, he roars for, arms in his bed and house he seeks;
sentences.i: beside himself, he shouts for his armour, hunts for his armour by the bed and through the house;
sentences.n: 'Arma… arma', anaphora at the head of each half of the line. 'Amens', 'out of his mind'. 'Fremit', 'roars', with the accusative of what he roars for. 'Toro tectisque', ablatives of place, 'in his bed and in the house'. The line recalls Aeneas's own madness on the night Troy fell, 'arma amens capio' (2.314).

sentences.t:
saevit amor ferri et scelerata insania belli,
ira super:
sentences.l:
rages the love of steel and the accursed madness of war,
anger over all:
sentences.i: a craving for the sword rages in him, and war's wicked madness, and over all of it, anger:
sentences.n: 'Saevit', 'rages', singular with two subjects, agreeing with the nearer, 'amor'. 'Ferri', 'of iron', 'of the sword'. 'Scelerata insania belli', 'the criminal madness of war': 'sceleratus' is 'wicked', 'accursed', for this is a war against the people the gods have sent. 'Ira super', 'anger on top', 'super' an adverb, with 'saevit' understood. The three subjects build to the last and shortest.

sentences.t:
magno veluti cum flamma sonore
virgea suggeritur costis undantis aëni
exsultantque aestu latices, furit intus aquaï
fumidus atque alte spumis exuberat amnis,
nec iam se capit unda, volat vapor ater ad auras.
sentences.l:
as when with great noise a flame
of brushwood is heaped under the ribs of a surging cauldron,
and leap with the heat the waters; rages within, of water,
smoking, and high with foam overflows, the stream,
and no longer itself contains the wave; flies a black vapour to the air.
sentences.i: just as when a fire of brushwood is piled roaring under the sides of a bubbling cauldron, and the water leaps with the heat, and the hot flood rages smoking within and boils up high in foam till the pot can hold it no longer, and dark steam flies up into the air.
sentences.n: A simile from the kitchen, as homely as the top (378–384). 'Veluti cum', 'as when'. 'Flamma… virgea', 'a flame of twigs', brushwood, which flares fast and loud ('magno… sonore'). 'Suggeritur', 'is heaped beneath'. 'Costis… aëni', 'under the ribs (sides) of the bronze', 'aënum' being the bronze pot; Greenough's diaeresis marks three syllables (familiar 'aeni'). 'Aquaï' is the archaic genitive in '-āī' (= 'aquae'), a deliberate Ennian archaism: 'aquai fumidus… amnis', 'the smoking river of water', is grand language for a potful. 'Se capit', 'holds itself'. The model is Iliad 21.362–365, where the river boils like a cauldron as Hephaestus's fire attacks it; Virgil turns it on a man's passion.

sentences.t:
Ergo iter ad regem polluta pace Latinum
indicit primis iuvenum et iubet arma parari,
tutari Italiam, detrudere finibus hostem:
sentences.l:
Therefore a march to the king, the peace defiled, Latinus,
he proclaims to the foremost of the youths, and orders arms to be readied,
to protect Italy, to thrust from its borders the enemy:
sentences.i: So, defiling the peace, he proclaims to the leaders of the young men a march on King Latinus, and orders arms to be made ready, to defend Italy and drive the enemy from its borders:
sentences.n: 'Ergo', 'so', 'accordingly'. 'Iter ad regem… Latinum', 'a march to King Latinus', framing the line; it is a march on him as much as to him. 'Polluta pace', an ablative absolute, 'the peace being defiled': most naturally the peace Latinus has just made with the Trojans' envoys, which this act breaks. 'Indicit', 'proclaims', the formal word for declaring war or ordering a march. 'Primis iuvenum', 'to the first of the young men', their leaders. 'Iubet' takes 'arma parari', 'arms to be prepared', and then, more loosely, 'tutari… detrudere', '(them) to defend… to thrust out'.

sentences.t: se satis ambobus Teucrisque venire Latinisque.
sentences.l: himself enough for both, Teucrians and Latins, comes.
sentences.i: he himself, he says, is a match for both, Teucrians and Latins alike.
sentences.n: Accusative and infinitive, depending on a verb of saying understood from 'indicit… iubet': '(he says) that he comes enough for both', that is, that he is a match for both; 'venire' here is close to 'esse'. 'Teucrisque… Latinisque', 'both Teucrians and Latins', the double '-que'. The line is hypermetric: its final '-que' is a syllable too many and elides into the vowel that opens the next line, 'Haec'. Virgil allows such lines rarely, almost always with '-que'. 'Teucris' is two syllables, as at 388.

sentences.t:
Haec ubi dicta dedit divosque in vota vocavit,
certatim sese Rutuli exhortantur in arma:
sentences.l:
These words when he had given and the gods to his vows had called,
in rivalry themselves the Rutulians urge on to arms:
sentences.i: When he had spoken so and called on the gods to hear his vows, the Rutulians vied with one another in urging themselves to arms:
sentences.n: 'Haec… dicta dedit', 'gave these words', 'said this', an epic formula. 'Divos in vota vocavit', 'called the gods to his vows', calling them to witness and promising offerings for success. 'Certatim', 'in rivalry', 'eagerly'. 'Sese… exhortantur', 'urge one another on', the reflexive used for a reciprocal act. 'Sēsē' is long-long, 'Rŭtŭli' short-short, its -i elided.

sentences.t:
hunc decus egregium formae movet atque iuventae,
hunc atavi reges, hunc claris dextera factis.
sentences.l:
this one the outstanding grace moves of his form and youth,
this one his ancestors, kings, this one his right hand, with its famous deeds.
sentences.i: one is stirred by his peerless beauty and youth, one by his line of royal ancestors, one by the right hand renowned for its deeds.
sentences.n: 'Hunc… hunc… hunc', 'this man… this man… this man', 'one… another… another', each of the Rutulians, the object of 'movet', understood in the second and third members. What moves them is Turnus's: 'decus egregium formae… atque iuventae', 'the outstanding grace of his form and youth'; 'atavi reges', 'his royal forebears' ('atavus', strictly a great-great-great-grandfather, here any ancestor); and 'claris dextera factis', 'his right hand, with its famous deeds', an ablative of quality. The tricolon closes the part on Turnus as his men see him: young, handsome, royal, proven. Allecto has one more task before her.
